name: S-300 / Buk-M1 (Soviet-legacy)

cost.display: Soviet-legacy stock, not purchased; no current market unit price

key_facts.label: Spec
key_facts.value: both radar-guided, pre-date modern Western networked SAM design

characteristics: both radar-guided, pre-date modern Western networked SAM design
Strength: Formed the backbone of Ukrainian air defense before Western systems arrived; large pre-war stockpile

Limitation: Radar-guided (more jammable than IR-seeking IRIS-T); missile stocks are finite with no ongoing Russian-sourced resupply; some S-300 units have been repurposed for surface-to-surface strikes late in the war due to interceptor shortages
Estimated quantity available: Pre-war inventory in the hundreds of launchers across S-300 variants; current operational count not fully public
employment_notes: Still carries a large share of the day-to-day air defense workload despite Western systems getting the attention; illustrates that legacy Soviet systems remain load-bearing infrastructure, not just a transitional stopgap
contrast_vs_traditional: Ukraine is defending its own skies with the same Soviet-lineage systems its adversary also still fields — both sides' air defense pictures descend from the same design family. Legacy point-defense doctrine assumed a belt of these systems could screen against a manned-aircraft threat; against a sky also full of cheap FPVs and one-way attack drones, no single belt of legacy SAMs was ever going to be dense enough on its own.

sources.label: Militarnyi — Ukraine's modernized Buk-M1 under FrankenSAM
